newsitem.title: UGANDA: Uganda says Zaire must change by peace or violence.
newsitem.headline: Uganda says Zaire must change by peace or violence.

text.p: Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni said a transformation of power in Zaire could not be delayed any longer and the question remained whether the process would be peaceful or violent.
"What is sure is that there will have to be transformation in the politics of Zaire -- the question is whether it will be peaceful or violent..." Museveni told a news conference on Monday.
"There will have to be democracy in Zaire. It cannot be postponed any longer," he said.
Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko's government has accused Museveni of backing and arming Laurent Kabila's rebels that now control more than half of the vast central African country.
Museveni has persistently denied the accusations.

Museveni rejected suggestions by reporters that he was building himself as a regional power broker and "King of the Great Lakes region" and said he offered no armed support to Kabila's rebels in Zaire or elsewhere.
Museveni said a venue for talks between Kabila and Mobutu had been identified by South African President Nelson Mandela.
He would not name the venue or a date for the talks, saying only that "Mr Mandela has made some arrangement where Mr Kabila will meet Mr Mobutu".
On Monday, Museveni told parliament that his forces had defeated Zairean and Sudanese troops that invaded Uganda last year and the security situation had "irreversibly improved".

He said the invasion last November of western Uganda from eastern Zaire was prompted by Sudanese spiritual leader Hassan al-Tourabi and facilitated by Zaire's corrupt army but these were stopped by Ugandan troops and Kabila's rebel soldiers.

"There was briefly an invasion of Kasese prompted by elements of the (rebel) Tabliqs led by one outlaw called Jamiru Mukulu, with prompting of Tourabi and facilitated by Mobutu's corrupt generals and governors in Kisangani and Kivu areas of Zaire," Museveni told parliament.
"Mobutu's backing of Mukulu's bandits was eliminated by the Banyamulenge (Kabila's soldiers) and the bandit bases were eliminated by UPDF (Uganda Peoples' Defence Forces) raids into Zaire."
Museveni indicated the only security problem for Uganda was in the north, the base for Joseph Kony's Christian fundamentallist Lord's Resistance Army (LRA).
Museveni said he was considering "justified violence" as a possible solution in ending the uprising in the north.
Museveni has previously accused Sudan of supporting LRA rebels while Khartoum accuses Kampala of backing the rebel South Sudan Peoples' Army (SPLA). Both governments deny these claims.
